edition.sessionCovered: Wed, Oct 28 close (post-FOMC) / Thu, Oct 29 early
edition.stripNote: Thu 29 Oct. Fed held 3.75–4.00% in a 10-2 vote — two members dissented for a hike. December hike probability 85%. Record 28 Hormuz attacks in October. US midterms Nov 3.
edition.scoreboardCaption: Thu 29 Oct early vs Wed 28 close. Ranked best to worst.

overview: Markets sold commodities and bought dollars on Thursday after the Federal Reserve held rates at 3.75–4.00% in a hawkish 10-2 split — Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack dissented, both wanting a quarter-point hike. The FOMC statement upgraded its growth assessment from 'solid' to 'strong,' and CME FedWatch now prices an 85% chance of a hike at the December 8–9 meeting, up from 73% before the decision. Chair Warsh said 'politics played no role' and that inflation 'remains elevated.' Brent crude eased 0.7% to $114.51 and WTI to $102 as the stronger dollar offset ongoing Hormuz supply fears — October set a record with 28 confirmed shipping attacks per the Washington Institute, with 11 VLCCs damaged. Newcastle coal firmed to $150.70. The US SPR remains at its 40-year low of 282.6 million barrels.

Gold led the post-FOMC selloff, falling 0.7% to $4,039 as the 10-year Treasury yield pushed back above 5% and the dollar strengthened. Silver slid 0.6% to $53.64, extending its worst month of the year. Copper bucked the trend at $6.66/lb, supported by the US-China trade thaw and mine supply disruptions. Bitcoin rallied to $81,500 as the hold decision provided relief, but the $82,000 resistance level and December hike overhang limited gains. Ethereum edged up to $2,350. Chinese lithium carbonate spot crossed back above the key ¥100,000 level to ¥100,050, a potential stabilisation signal after last week's breach. Grains remained under pressure: wheat slid to 601¢ and soybeans to 1,222¢, while corn held flat at 452¢.

watchItems.title: December FOMC: 85% hike probability
watchItems.text: The December 8–9 FOMC meeting is now the key event, with futures pricing an 85% chance of another quarter-point hike to 4.00–4.25%. The meeting will include an updated Summary of Economic Projections and dot plot — the October meeting had neither. Markets now expect the fed funds rate to reach roughly 4.7% by September 2027, implying three more hikes. Goldman Sachs and Russell Investments both expect a December increase if inflation doesn't meaningfully cool.

watchItems.title: US midterm elections November 3
watchItems.text: The US midterm elections on Tuesday, November 3 could shift the fiscal policy backdrop. Control of Congress affects spending authorisation, defense budgets, trade policy tools, and the legislative path for any Iran-related sanctions. Markets are also watching whether election results change the dynamics of US engagement in the Hormuz conflict. Chair Warsh explicitly stated that politics played 'no role' in the October rate decision.

watchItems.title: Hormuz record October — November trajectory
watchItems.text: October closed with 28 confirmed shipping attacks near the Strait of Hormuz — the highest monthly total since the Washington Institute began tracking in 2017. Eleven VLCCs were damaged, about 3.5% of the global fleet. Iran's IRGC claimed seven vessel strikes on October 22 alone. UKMTO has logged over 135 conflict-related incidents since February 28. Shipowners still load inside the Gulf, drawn by daily freight rates above $1 million, but the rate of fleet damage is accelerating. November trajectory is the critical question.

watchItems.title: Lithium crosses back above ¥100,000
watchItems.text: Chinese lithium carbonate spot edged to ¥100,050 per tonne, reclaiming the psychologically important ¥100,000 level that was broken for the first time last week. Futures remain near ¥94,000, roughly halved from the mid-May peak above ¥200,000. Goldman Sachs projects the market flipping from a 404,000-tonne deficit in 2026 to a 444,000-tonne surplus by 2028. Whether the spot market can hold above ¥100,000 will signal whether the long decline has found a floor.

desk.name: Gold
desk.sum: Gold fell 0.7% to $4,039 on Thursday as the hawkish FOMC outcome lifted the dollar and pushed the 10-year yield back above 5%. The Fed held rates in a 10-2 vote, with two members wanting a hike. The statement upgraded growth from 'solid' to 'strong,' and December hike probability rose to 85%. The metal is now about 28% below its January record near $5,608.

desk.name: Silver
desk.sum: Silver fell 0.6% to $53.64 on Thursday, extending its post-FOMC decline alongside gold. The metal is down about 15% on the month, making it one of the worst-performing commodities in October. The gold-silver ratio widened to approximately 75.3.

desk.name: Oil
desk.sum: Brent pulled back 0.7% to $114.51 on Thursday as the post-FOMC dollar rally weighed on crude. WTI fell similarly to $102. The hawkish tone and stronger dollar offset supply concerns from the Hormuz conflict, which set a monthly record with 28 confirmed attacks in October. The US SPR remains at a 40-year low of 282.6 million barrels. Shipowners still load inside the Gulf, drawn by daily freight rates above $1 million.

desk.name: Copper
desk.sum: Copper firmed 0.2% to $6.66 per pound on Thursday, bucking the post-FOMC commodities selloff. The metal continues to find support from easing US-China trade tensions and supply disruptions at the Grasberg mine in Indonesia and Codelco's El Teniente in Chile.

desk.name: Coal
desk.sum: Newcastle coal firmed 0.5% to $150.70, holding near its recent range. The IEA forecasts record global coal demand of 8.94 billion tonnes this year. Asian utilities remain dependent on coal as the Hormuz crisis disrupts LNG supply chains. Indonesia, the largest exporter, cut its production target with shipments running below 2025 levels.

desk.name: Platinum
desk.sum: Platinum eased 0.3% to $1,535 on Thursday, slipping alongside gold after the hawkish FOMC outcome. The metal remains down about 11% on the month as elevated yields and a firm dollar weigh on the PGM complex. WPIC's forecast of an 18% drop in total platinum demand this year continues to cap rallies.

desk.name: Palladium
desk.sum: Palladium was essentially flat at $1,015 on Thursday, holding near multi-month lows. The metal is down about 22% on the month. Platinum substitution in gasoline catalysts and growing EV market share continue to structurally weigh on demand.

desk.name: Hormuz Terminal
desk.m: ~30 transits/day vs 85 pre-war · 28 attacks in Oct
desk.sum: October closed with a record 28 confirmed attacks on shipping near the Strait of Hormuz per the Washington Institute — the highest monthly total since tracking began in 2017. Eleven VLCCs were damaged, about 3.5% of the global fleet. Iran's IRGC claimed seven vessel strikes on October 22 alone. UKMTO has logged over 135 conflict-related incidents since February 28. US-facilitated transits remain above 30 per day, still far below the pre-war baseline of 85. US midterm elections on November 3 add further political uncertainty to the conflict trajectory.

desk.name: Corn
desk.sum: December corn was essentially flat at 452 cents on Thursday, barely changed after the FOMC decision. Managed money still holds substantial short positions in corn. The US corn harvest continues near the five-year average pace.

desk.name: Wheat
desk.sum: December wheat edged up 0.35% to 601 cents on Thursday but remains down about 16% on the month, its weakest October level in years. The post-FOMC dollar rally added to pressure from record managed-money short positions and adequate global supply. Winter wheat planting remains on schedule.

desk.name: Soybean
desk.sum: November soybeans slipped 0.2% to 1,222 cents on Thursday. The US harvest continues to run ahead of the five-year average, pointing to a record crop. Brazilian production estimates remain robust, adding to the bearish supply outlook.

desk.name: Cryptocurrencies
desk.sum: Bitcoin rallied to $81,500 on Thursday, its highest level in over a week, as the Fed's decision to hold rates provided relief to risk assets. However, the hawkish split vote — two members dissenting for a hike — and 85% December hike probability cap the upside. The $82,000 level remains key resistance with $80,000 as support. Ethereum edged up to $2,350.

desk.name: LNG
desk.sum: Asian LNG spot (JKM) held near $31.50 per MMBtu on Thursday, consolidating after recent gains. Hormuz disruption continues to threaten Qatar's 106 million tonnes of annual LNG export capacity. European TTF held near €97 per MWh. Henry Hub fell 0.7% to $3.01, and the gap between US and global spot markets remains wide.

desk.name: Sulfur
desk.sum: Sulfur remains elevated with CFR Southeast Asia around $1,100–1,300 per tonne. Chinese sulfuric acid (98%) traded at 1,647 yuan per tonne in mid-October per NBS data, down 2.9% on the period. Middle East FOB prices hold near $765. Hormuz disruption continues squeezing sulfuric acid supply chains — the essential input for copper leaching, phosphate fertilizer, and oil refining.

desk.name: Potash
desk.m: Down from $396 in Jul · China port MOP ¥2,898
desk.sum: Muriate of potash (MOP) CFR Brazil holds near $367 per tonne, little changed. Chinese domestic port MOP fell 5.3% to 2,898 yuan per tonne in mid-October per NBS data. Belarus and Russia still account for about 40% of global supply despite Western sanctions, routing through non-aligned buyers.

desk.name: Antimony
desk.sum: Chinese antimony (#1 ingot) held near 90,000 yuan per tonne, consolidating after October's sharp correction from the 105,000 yuan post-holiday high. SMM reports the price dropped 12.4% in the week of October 12–16, settling at 92,000 yuan, before stabilising in the final two weeks of the month. Supply remains structurally tight but demand from flame retardant and PV glass sectors is subdued.

desk.name: Gallium & Germanium
desk.m: China exports −94% since controls · domestic Ga ¥1,740/kg
desk.sum: Gallium remains near a record $1,850 per kilogram outside China, up over 200% since early 2025. Chinese domestic gallium trades at 1,740 yuan per kilogram. Beijing's Document No. 46 export controls retain a presumption of denial for US end users, and the Busan truce's Document No. 72 suspension has not meaningfully restored exports. China produces about 98% of global gallium and 60% of germanium.

desk.name: Vanadium
desk.sum: Vanadium pentoxide (V₂O₅) averaged about $5.02 per pound in 2025, slipping from $5.44 in 2024 as steel demand softened. The long-term bull case rests on vanadium redox flow batteries (VRFBs) for grid-scale energy storage. China, Russia and South Africa control over 90% of supply.

desk.name: Cocoa
desk.sum: ICE cocoa fell 2.1% to $5,462 per tonne, retreating from recent gains. Rising Ivory Coast arrivals — up 19.8% in the current marketing year — and ICE inventories at a 2.25-year high continue to weigh on prices. El Niño forecasts affecting West African producers into 2027 limit the downside.

desk.name: Cobalt
desk.sum: Cobalt traded at $34,620 per tonne, roughly steady. The DRC (70% of global mine supply) maintains export quotas of 96,600 tonnes per year to support prices, but the EV battery chemistry shift from NMC to LFP continues to structurally reduce demand. Aerospace and superalloy uses provide a floor.

desk.name: Lithium
desk.sum: Chinese lithium carbonate spot edged up 0.7% to ¥100,050 per tonne, crossing back above the key ¥100,000 level that was breached for the first time last week. Futures remain near ¥94,000, roughly halved from the mid-May peak above ¥200,000. Goldman Sachs projects the global market flipping from a 404,000-tonne deficit in 2026 to a 444,000-tonne surplus by 2028.

desk.name: Rubber
desk.sum: Natural rubber (RSS3) trades around $2,550 per tonne ($2.55/kg), easing modestly. Southeast Asian supply remains tight with Thailand, Indonesia and Malaysia — producing 70% of global latex — still affected by fungal leaf blight (Pestalotiopsis). Auto-sector demand remains solid.
